title: Trendline Break
teaches: The trendline break as we trade it: a leader above its 200-day drifts tight under a falling line drawn over the daily highs, the buy is the trade through the line and the prior day's high at market in regular hours and never more than 4% past the line, the stop sits a few cents under the trigger day's low, a close back under the line is a warning and not an exit, a third comes off at 3R and 5R with the rest on the trail, and a break on its own is a warning, not a reversal.

facts.quote: A downtrend line has a negative slope formed by connecting two or more high points.
facts.claim: ChartSchool: a downtrend line slopes down and connects high points.

facts.quote: As the steepness of a trend line increases, the validity of the support or resistance level decreases.
facts.claim: ChartSchool: the steeper the line, the less valid it is.

facts.quote: Trend line breaks should not be the final arbiter, but should serve merely as a warning that a change in trend may be imminent.
facts.claim: ChartSchool: a break is a warning, not the final arbiter.

facts.quote: Sometimes, the lows or highs don't match up, and it is best not to force the issue.
facts.claim: ChartSchool: when the highs do not match up, do not force the line.

facts.quote: If the points of contact between price and trendlines are too close, the move might be nothing more than noise.
facts.claim: The Insider: touches too close together may be nothing more than noise.

facts.quote: Stop first (by default a few cents under the day's low or the prior day's low, F62); the size comes from the stop; if the honest stop does not fit the risk, skip the trade.

facts.claim: A4: the stop is the exit; it only moves up, never wider; the gap rule is the one exception.

questions.q: Our falling trendline for a breakout is drawn over what?
choices: The daily highs, wicks included
The daily closes, not the wicks
The daily lows of the pullback
The 50-day moving average line
questions.why: The daily highs, wicks included. Our card draws the line over the daily highs of the pullback, wicks and all. It starts at the pullback's highest high, on a log chart. ChartSchool says a downtrend line connects two or more high points. Bulkowski draws a down-sloping line above the peaks, not below the valleys. It is not drawn on the closes or along an average.
questions.lesson_line: Draw it over the highs, wicks and all. Start at the pullback's highest high.

wrong.The daily closes, not the wicks: A line over the closes cuts through the wicks. The line goes over the highs.
wrong.The 50-day moving average line: An average is not a trendline. The line is drawn on the highs themselves.
wrong.The daily lows of the pullback: A line under the lows is support. A falling line for a breakout sits above the peaks, not below the valleys.

questions.simple: Draw the falling line over the daily highs, wicks and all, because a downtrend line connects the high points.

reasons: rests on a proposed criteria card line awaiting the owner (tl.line_drawn); two web publishers agree

questions.q: On its own, a trendline break is a warning, not a reversal.
questions.why: True. ChartSchool says a trend line break should serve merely as a warning that a change in trend may be imminent. The Insider calls it a heads-up. Our card names treating any break as a reversal as a mistake.
questions.lesson_line: A broken line is a heads-up. It is not a reversal by itself.
questions.simple: True, a broken line only warns that the trend may change, and it does not prove a reversal.

reasons: +2 tied to D-002 (standalone setup or trigger); the warning line itself holds under every option and four sources agree

questions.q: Where does the stop go on a trendline break bought during the day?
choices: A few cents under the day's low
Exactly on the falling line itself
Under the 200-day average line
A fixed 8% below the buy price
questions.answer: A few cents under the day's low
questions.why: A few cents under the trigger day's low, as it stands at entry. Not exactly on the low, and not on the line. The prior day's low is the wider choice the rulebook also allows. The stop comes first, and the size comes from it.
questions.lesson_line: Stop first: a few cents under the trigger day's low.

wrong.Exactly on the falling line itself: The line is the trigger, not the stop. A close back under it is a warning; the stop is the exit.
wrong.Under the 200-day average line: That is far below the trade. The stop sits close, near the trigger day's low.
wrong.A fixed 8% below the buy price: Our stop comes from the chart, not a set percent. It usually sits within about 3% of the buy.

questions.simple: Put the stop a few cents under the low of the day you buy, and size the trade from that stop.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (A3, F62)

+2 rests on the owner's rulebook (A5, no adding)

questions.q: Raising the stop as the break works is fine, if the new stop is still a real order with the broker.
questions.why: True. The stop only moves up, never down or wider. It sits with the broker as a real stop order, not a stop kept in your head. Raising it is allowed, lowering or widening it is not. The one exception is the gap rule.
questions.lesson_line: Raise it if the trade works. Keep it a real order.
questions.simple: True, you may raise the stop as the trade works, as long as it stays a real order with your broker.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (A4, D41)
+1 fixed before (2026-11-11 flagged-question fix)

questions.q: Which event is the buy on a trendline break?
choices: Trades through the line and prior high
Price touches the line from below
Volume jumps, still under the line
The 50-day crossing the 200-day
questions.answer: Trades through the line and prior high
questions.why: It trades through the line's value for the day and above the prior day's high, during regular hours, bought at market. That is our default trigger. A touch from below is not a break.
questions.lesson_line: Through the line and the prior high, in hours, at market.

wrong.Price touches the line from below: Touching the line is not a break. Price has to trade through it.
wrong.Volume jumps, still under the line: Volume alone is not the buy. Price has to trade through the line and the prior day's high.
wrong.The 50-day crossing the 200-day: A crossing of averages is a different signal. The trigger is the line and the prior high.

questions.simple: The buy is when price trades through the line and above the prior day's high during market hours.

deeper.trap: A touch of the line from below can look like the start. It is not a break. Our default buys when price trades through the line's value and the prior day's high, at market, in regular hours.

reasons: +2 rests on a held decision (D-003, the entry event)
+1 fixed before (the old why ruled the close out as settled)

questions.q: We wait for a close 3% past the line before we buy.
questions.why: False. Do not wait for a close 3% past the line. That filter is for long-term lines and would use up most of the 4% chase limit.
questions.lesson_line: No 3% filter. Waiting costs most of the chase limit.

questions.q: Two highs fix a falling line. How far apart should they be?
choices: At least 5 sessions
Any two highs work
At least 20 days
3 sessions or more
questions.why: At least 5 sessions. That is our working rule, a proposal on the card. The Insider says that if the points of contact are too close, the move might be nothing more than noise. Highs side by side do not make a line you can trust.
questions.lesson_line: Space the anchors out. Two highs a few days apart prove nothing.

wrong.Any two highs work: Highs side by side may be nothing more than noise. Our card asks for at least 5 sessions.
wrong.At least 20 days: Our card's floor is 5 sessions, not 20.
wrong.3 sessions or more: Our card asks for at least 5 sessions, so 3 falls short of our rule.

questions.simple: Space the two highs at least 5 sessions apart, because touches too close together may just be noise.

reasons: +2 the 5 sessions is the card's proposal, tied to D-068 in the lesson's conflicts
+2 a number that may change when the owner rules
+1 fixed before (reworded so the number reads as ours)

questions.q: A wick through the line before the trigger day cancels the first break.
questions.why: False. A first break means no daily close above the line before the trigger day. A wick through is allowed.
questions.lesson_line: Closes count, wicks do not. No close above the line before the trigger.

questions.q: We take trendline breaks only in stocks at $10 or more that trade $20 million a day.
questions.why: True. Our rule for every setup: only stocks at $10 or more that trade at least $20 million a day. A clean line in a thin stock is still a thin stock.
questions.lesson_line: A clean line in a thin stock is still a thin stock.
questions.simple: True, we only trade stocks at $10 or more that trade at least $20 million a day.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (B23)

questions.q: How far over its 10-day average is too far to buy a break?
choices: More than 10%
More than 25%
More than 5%
More than 2%
questions.why: More than 10%. Our rule: skip a long that is more than 10% above its 10-day average, measured on the trigger day. Under that line, the break can be bought if every other rule passes.
questions.lesson_line: Stretched is a pass. More than 10% over the 10-day, skip it.

wrong.More than 25%: That bar is too high. Our rule skips anything more than 10% over the 10-day, well before 25%.

questions.simple: Skip the buy when the stock is more than 10% over its 10-day average, because it is too stretched.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (C29)

questions.q: It helps when the index itself is breaking its own downtrend line.
questions.why: True. The index breaking its own downtrend line or making a wedge pop is a cue. Kell: as the index pops, the strongest stocks break out.
questions.lesson_line: Best when the market breaks its own line too.

questions.q: Which market reading allows a full-size trendline break?
choices: Green
Yellow
Orange
Red
questions.why: Green. The market reading is a guide, not a hard cap. Green means full risk per grade and up to 10 positions. Yellow is smaller and fewer, Orange takes A+ setups only, and Red is mostly cash and shorts.
questions.lesson_line: Green is full size. The other readings cut size or the setups you take.

wrong.Yellow: Yellow is smaller and fewer, not full size.
wrong.Red: Red is mostly cash and shorts.

questions.simple: Green allows full size, because each of the other readings cuts the size or limits which trades you take.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (F65)

questions.q: Bought at 26.97 with the stop at 26.73. Where is 3R?
questions.why: 27.69. One R is the fill minus the stop, 26.97 minus 26.73. Add three of those to the fill and you get 27.69. A third comes off there. MSFT traded there the next session.
questions.lesson_line: Know your 3R before the open. The first third comes off there.
questions.simple: 3R is 27.69, because you add three times the gap between the buy and the stop to the buy.

reasons: +2 computed key
+2 rests on the owner's rulebook (B19, a third at 3R)

questions.q: The line is at 50.00, and 1.5 ATR is 3.00. What is the most we pay?
questions.why: 52.00. Our rule: never buy more than 4% above the buy point. On a trendline break that is the line's value, and 50.00 times 1.04 is 52.00. The card also caps a buy at 1.5 ATR over the line, whichever is smaller. Here 1.5 ATR is the wider cap, so the 4% decides.
questions.lesson_line: Four percent over the line is the limit. Chasing costs size.
questions.simple: The most is 52.00, because 4% over the 50.00 line is the tighter of our two caps here.

reasons: +2 computed key
+2 rests on the owner's rulebook (C28)
+1 fixed before (now gives the ATR so the 4% and the 1.5 ATR caps agree)

questions.q: After entry, a close back under the line means sell at once.
questions.why: False. After the entry, a close back under the line is a warning, not an exit. The stop is the exit, and it only moves up.
questions.lesson_line: A close under the line is a warning. The stop is the exit.
questions.simple: False, a close back under the line is only a warning, and the stop order is what gets you out.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (A4)

questions.q: Which lead-in to the line is best?
choices: Tight drift down, volume drying up
Quiet drift, closes well below the line
Wide, loose swings under the line
One big, fast drop off the high
questions.answer: Tight drift down, volume drying up
questions.why: A tight drift down on drying volume. Our card wants the closes of the 5 sessions before the trigger within about 5% under the line. The average daily range should be smaller than the 20-session average. Wide swings are not tight. A big, fast drop makes a steep line, and a steeper line is less valid.
questions.lesson_line: Tight and quiet, just under the line.

wrong.Quiet drift, closes well below the line: Tight means the closes sit within about 5% under the line, not far below it.
wrong.Wide, loose swings under the line: Wide swings are not tight. The average daily range should shrink.
wrong.One big, fast drop off the high: A big, fast drop makes a steep line. The steeper the line, the less valid it is.

questions.simple: A tight, quiet drift down just under the line is best, because we want closes near the line and a shrinking range.

reasons: rests on a proposed criteria card line awaiting the owner (tl.tight_under, tl.not_wedging_up)

questions.q: Tap the number that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: A steadier stock's last third trails on a close under the ___-day.
questions.why: 21. Our default trail is the 21-day average for a steadier stock and the 10-day for a fast mover. Sell on a close below it. This trail is for the last third, after a third comes off at 3R and another at 5R.
questions.lesson_line: Steadier stock, 21-day. Fast mover, 10-day. Sell the close below it, not the touch.
questions.simple: A steadier stock's last third trails the 21-day average, and we sell it on a close below that line.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (E52)

questions.q: Into a vertical climax burst, we sell a big part of the position.
questions.why: True. A climax burst on the way up is for selling into. It is a judgment call, and selling a big part is the rule.
questions.lesson_line: A burst up is for selling into. Take the money.

questions.q: A stock sits under falling 10 and 21-day averages that act as resistance. What is a line break there?
choices: Not this setup; pass on it
A buy once it clears the line
Fine if the volume is big
Pass; its stop is too wide
questions.answer: Not this setup; pass on it
questions.why: Not this setup. Our card rules out a stock that sits under falling averages acting as resistance before the entry. Kell says it is best to avoid a downtrend when the moving averages act as resistance, guiding the stock lower. A trendline break wants the fast averages already reclaimed or held on the trigger day.
questions.lesson_line: Under falling averages that act as resistance: not this setup.

wrong.A buy once it clears the line: Falling averages overhead act as resistance. The card rules this out before any break.
wrong.Fine if the volume is big: Volume does not fix a stock under falling averages. The card rules it out before any break.
wrong.Pass; its stop is too wide: The story says nothing about the stop. The card rules this stock out for the falling averages overhead.

questions.simple: Pass, because a stock pushed lower by falling averages is not this setup, even if it pokes through a line.

reasons: rests on a proposed criteria card line awaiting the owner (tl.inv_falling_mas)
Kell quote is an Internet Archive capture this writer could not reach

questions.q: If the highs do not line up, we draw the line through the closest points anyway.
questions.why: False. ChartSchool says when the lows or highs do not match up, it is best not to force the issue. The CMT Association says proper trendlines should never be forced. If no line fits the highs cleanly, there is no line to break.
questions.lesson_line: No line, no trade. Never force a line through the points.
questions.simple: False. If the highs do not line up, we do not force a line, and with no clean line there is no trade.

reasons: stable drawing rule; two publishers agree

questions.q: Bought at 109.23 with the stop at 106.79. How far below the buy is the stop, in percent?
questions.why: 2.23%. Take the buy minus the stop, divide by the buy, and times 100. That is inside the about 3% a stop usually sits within. Know this distance before you size the trade.
questions.lesson_line: Buy minus stop, over the buy. Know the distance before you size.
questions.simple: The stop is 2.23% below the buy, which is inside the about 3% where a stop usually sits.

reasons: +2 computed key
+2 rests on the owner's rulebook (A13)

questions.q: Buy the open?
questions.story: The falling line sits at 40.00 today. News gaps the stock open to 41.80.
choices: Pass; 4.5% over the line
Buy at market; it has momentum
Buy half size; less to lose
Buy; the open is above the line
questions.why: Pass. A gap open more than 4% above the line is no trade, and 41.80 is 4.5% over 40.00. Our rulebook says never buy more than 4% above the buy point.
questions.lesson_line: More than 4% over the line is no trade. Let it go.

wrong.Buy at market; it has momentum: Momentum does not lift the cap. A gap open more than 4% over the line is no trade.
wrong.Buy half size; less to lose: Half of a chase is still a chase. A gap open more than 4% over the line is no trade.
wrong.Buy; the open is above the line: Above the line is not enough. A gap open more than 4% over the line is no trade.

questions.simple: Pass, because the stock opened 4.5% over the line, and a gap open more than 4% over it is no trade.

reasons: +2 computed key
+2 rests on the owner's rulebook (C28) and the card's gap line

questions.q: Buy the next break?
questions.story: Your break was stopped on Monday. On Wednesday the stock makes a new high, and you redraw the line through it.
choices: No; a redrawn line is no trigger
Yes; the new line is cleaner
Yes, with a tighter stop
questions.answer: No; a redrawn line is no trigger
questions.why: No. After a stop-out, buy again only on a new trigger. Do not redraw the same line to get back in.
questions.lesson_line: A stop-out is not a reason to redraw the line.

wrong.Yes; the new line is cleaner: Redrawing the line to get back in is the named mistake.
wrong.Yes, with a tighter stop: Tightening the stop does not make a redrawn line a trigger.

questions.q: Is this our trendline break?
questions.story: A stock 20% under its 200-day breaks a 60-session falling line on twice its usual volume.
choices: No; it is under the 200-day
Yes; the volume is big
Yes, if the line is long
questions.why: No. The trigger day must close above the 200-day, and we do not buy longs below it. A long line and big volume do not change that.
questions.lesson_line: The 200-day comes first. A beaten-down stock is not our break.

wrong.Yes; the volume is big: Big volume does not lift a stock over its 200-day.
wrong.Yes, if the line is long: A long line does not change the 200-day rule.

questions.q: Which setup is this?
questions.story: Three highs sit at exactly 50.00 over six weeks. You are weighing a buy through 50.00.
choices: A flat-top break, no slope
A descending trendline break
A wedge pop off the lows
No setup; a ceiling is no buy
questions.why: A flat top. A trendline falls, at least a little, from lower swing highs. Three highs at exactly 50.00 have no slope. A line with no slope is a horizontal resistance break, not this setup. A flat top is a setup of its own, judged by its own rules.
questions.lesson_line: No slope, no trendline. Three equal highs are a flat top.

wrong.A descending trendline break: The highs are level, so there is no falling line to break.
wrong.A wedge pop off the lows: A wedge pop needs a decline with most closes under the 20 EMA first. Level highs at 50.00 are a ceiling.
wrong.No setup; a ceiling is no buy: A flat base has its own buy, the base's highest high. It is just not a trendline break.

questions.simple: It is a flat top, because the three highs are level, and a trendline break needs a line that falls.

reasons: rests on a proposed criteria card line awaiting the owner (the lookalike tell); the slope number is held (D-069) and never keyed

questions.q: Bought at 26.97, stop 26.73. The stock trades to 28.17. How many R is that?
questions.why: 5R. One R is the fill minus the stop. Divide the gain, 28.17 minus 26.97, by that R and you get 5.0. That is where the second third comes off. The rulebook calls that level adjustable.
questions.lesson_line: Count in R, not dollars. 5R is the second trim.
questions.simple: It is 5R, because the gain from the buy is five times the gap between the buy and the stop.

reasons: +2 computed key
+2 rests on the owner's rulebook (E51)

questions.q: The stop moves to breakeven somewhere between 2R and 5R.
questions.why: True. Our rulebook moves the stop to breakeven at 2R to 5R, ideally. The card does it at the first trim by default, and the hard rule for that trim is a third at 3R. The stop only moves up, never down or wider.
questions.lesson_line: Breakeven between 2R and 5R, at the first trim.
questions.simple: True, the stop moves to breakeven somewhere from 2R to 5R, by default when we sell the first third.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B19)

questions.q: What does the index break do for your list?
questions.story: The S&P 500 breaks its own downtrend line on a strong day. Your list holds three valid line breaks.
choices: A cue to look harder at them
Nothing; indexes do not matter
Skip them; the move is already late
Double the size on all three
questions.answer: A cue to look harder at them
questions.why: A cue to look harder. Our card lists the index breaking its own downtrend line, or making a wedge pop, as a cue for this setup. Kell says the strongest stocks break out from their bases as the index forms a wedge pop. A cue is a reason to look, not a rule. Each stock still needs its own trigger, stop and size.
questions.lesson_line: An index breaking its own line is a cue to look at the leaders.

wrong.Nothing; indexes do not matter: The market reading is a guide for every trade, and the index break is a cue for this setup.
wrong.Skip them; the move is already late: The card lists the index break as a cue for this setup. It is a reason to look, not to skip.
wrong.Double the size on all three: No rule doubles size on a cue. Shares come from the account, the risk percent and the stop.

questions.simple: It is a cue to look harder, because our card lists an index breaking its own line as a cue.

reasons: rests on a proposed criteria card line awaiting the owner (tl.index_break)
Kell quote is an Internet Archive capture this writer could not reach

questions.q: Which level does our card call overhead supply on a line break?
choices: The old high where the line starts
The prior day's high at the trigger
The 3R trim level above the buy
The 200-day simple moving average
questions.answer: The old high where the line starts
questions.why: The old high where the line starts. Our card calls the first anchor high overhead supply. It is context, not a rule. On a break, the prior day's high and the 200-day sit under the price, and 3R is a trim level.
questions.lesson_line: The anchor high is overhead. Know where it is before you buy.

wrong.The prior day's high at the trigger: The trigger trades above the prior day's high, so it sits under the price. Supply is the old high.
wrong.The 3R trim level above the buy: 3R is a trim level set from your own stop, not supply. Supply is the old high where the line starts.
wrong.The 200-day simple moving average: A stock we buy closes above its 200-day, so the 200-day is under the price, not overhead.

questions.simple: The old high where the line starts, because our card calls that first anchor high overhead supply.

reasons: rests on a proposed criteria card line awaiting the owner (tl.overhead_supply)
a study statistic (77%) that a revised page could change

questions.q: Which is the setup, and which is the trigger?
questions.story: A stock jumps 25% in 20 sessions, then drifts for 8 sessions under a falling line of two highs.
choices: Flag is the setup, line the trigger
Line is the setup; flag is the context
Two setups, so two separate trades
Wedge pop is the setup; line the trigger
questions.answer: Flag is the setup, line the trigger
questions.why: The flag is the setup and the line is its trigger. Our card says so whenever the line is the top of a flag. A bull flag needs a 20% pole in the 20 sessions before and a pause of 3 to 15 sessions. This stock jumped 25% in 20 sessions, then paused for 8. It is one entry: full size once, one stop.
questions.lesson_line: The flag is the setup. The line is how you get in.

wrong.Line is the setup; flag is the context: When the line is the top of a flag, the flag is the setup and the line is its trigger.
wrong.Two setups, so two separate trades: One structure, one trade, one stop. A break is never an add.
wrong.Wedge pop is the setup; line the trigger: A wedge pop comes after a decline, with most closes under the 20 EMA. This stock jumped 25% first.

questions.simple: The flag is the setup and the falling line on top of it is the trigger, so it is one trade.

reasons: rests on a proposed criteria card line awaiting the owner (the flag lookalike)
the standalone-or-trigger question is held (D-002)

questions.q: Which setup is this?
questions.story: A stock closed 12 of the last 15 sessions under its 20 EMA. A bar then clears a 4-day tight range and both fast averages.
choices: A wedge pop off a decline
A trendline break; it cleared a range
A flat-top break at a ceiling
A launchpad off the fast averages
questions.answer: A wedge pop off a decline
questions.why: A wedge pop. On our card, a wedge pop follows a decline with at least 8 of the last 15 closes under the 20 EMA. It leaves a tight range of 3 days or more and reclaims the 10 and 20 EMAs. Here 12 of 15 closed under it, out of a 4-day range. A trendline break has its fast EMAs already reclaimed or held.
questions.lesson_line: Lost the averages, then reclaimed them: that is the pop.

wrong.A flat-top break at a ceiling: A flat top is one level touched twice. The tell here is the closes under the 20 EMA, then the reclaim.
wrong.A trendline break; it cleared a range: A trendline break has its fast averages already reclaimed or held. Here this bar is the one that takes them back.
wrong.A launchpad off the fast averages: A launchpad is the 8, 21 and 50-day pinched near the 200-day. The story names only the fast pair and the closes under the 20 EMA.

questions.simple: It is a wedge pop: most recent closes sat under the 20 EMA, and this bar takes the averages back.

reasons: +3 one source only (the card's lookalike lines c40, c41)
+1 fixed before

questions.q: Take it?
questions.story: The reading is Orange. A valid break has a stop 6% away, and a key level sits just above.
choices: No; it does not grade A+
Yes; the line itself is valid
Yes; take it at half size
No; Orange means no new trades
questions.answer: No; it does not grade A+
questions.why: No. In an Orange market we take only A+ setups. A 6% stop and a key level just above are both lower-grade marks on the card. A valid line is not enough, and half size does not lift the grade.
questions.lesson_line: In an Orange market, only the best setups get through.

wrong.No; Orange means no new trades: Orange still takes A+ setups. This one is a pass because it does not grade A+.
wrong.Yes; the line itself is valid: A valid line is not enough in Orange. It has to grade A+.
wrong.Yes; take it at half size: Half size does not make it an A+. Orange takes A+ only.

questions.simple: No, because an Orange market takes only A+ setups, and a 6% stop with a key level just above grades lower.

deeper.trap: A valid line is not the same as a good setup. In Orange the question is the grade, not the line. A wide stop and a key level just overhead both point away from A+, so it is a pass at any size.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (F65)
+1 fixed before (threshold wording removed, E50)

questions.q: What do you do?
questions.story: The honest stop sits 4.5% under the buy. Your usual size would risk too much.
choices: Take the smaller size, or skip
Tighten the stop to 3% to fit
Use full size and accept the risk
Buy half now, add the rest later
questions.answer: Take the smaller size, or skip
questions.why: Take the smaller size the formula gives, or skip. The stop comes first, and the size comes from the stop. Shares are the account times the risk percent, divided by entry minus stop, rounded down. A 4.5% stop gives fewer shares for the same risk. If the honest stop does not fit, skip. Never tighten the stop to fit the size.
questions.lesson_line: The stop sets the size. Never back-fit a tighter stop.

wrong.Tighten the stop to 3% to fit: Tightening the honest stop to fit the size is the mistake. The size moves, not the stop.
wrong.Use full size and accept the risk: Full size on a wide stop risks more than the rule allows.
wrong.Buy half now, add the rest later: A break is a first entry, never an add. The size is bought once, at one price, with one stop.

questions.simple: Buy fewer shares or skip it, because the stop sets the size, and we never pull the stop closer just to fit.

deeper.example: Say your usual size was built for a stop about 3% away. With the honest stop at 4.5%, the same risk buys fewer shares. That smaller size is the right size. Pulling the stop in to 3% keeps the shares but puts the stop where the chart does not say it belongs.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A3, A5) and the card's stop width line

questions.q: Which does this trade match?
questions.story: A break barely clears the line, closing 0.4% over it on thin volume. You buy it, stop a few cents under the day's low. Next day it closes back under, and the stop trades.
choices: The card's named failure mode
A stop set too tight for the line
A buy past the 4% chase limit
Proof the setup does not work
questions.why: The card's named failure mode. Our card lists it: a weak-volume break that barely clears the line closes back under it the next day, and the stop goes. The stop is the exit, so the trade ends there.
questions.lesson_line: A barely-there break on thin volume is the card's failure mode.

wrong.A stop set too tight for the line: The stop sat a few cents under the day's low, as the rule says. The weak spot was the break.
wrong.A buy past the 4% chase limit: The close was only 0.4% over the line, well inside the 4% limit.
wrong.Proof the setup does not work: One loss proves nothing. This is the failure our card names, a weak break.

questions.simple: It matches the failure our card names: a thin-volume break that barely clears the line falls back, and the stop goes.

reasons: +2 tied to D-069 (volume as a gate or a cue); the key holds under either
+1 fixed before

questions.q: What do you do?
questions.story: You bought a break 11 trading days ago. It sits at 0.6R after three flat closes with no higher high.
choices: Sell; it is under 1R too long
Hold; the stop has not traded
Add more; it is holding up
Raise the stop to breakeven
questions.answer: Sell; it is under 1R too long
questions.why: Sell. Our time stop: a trade still under 1R after 10 trading days is sold, freeing the money. This one is 11 trading days in at 0.6R. No follow-through within a few sessions is itself the signal. A stop that has not traded does not keep a dead trade alive.
questions.lesson_line: No follow-through is the signal. Free the money.

wrong.Hold; the stop has not traded: The time stop is its own exit. Under 1R after 10 trading days, the money goes elsewhere.
wrong.Add more; it is holding up: A break is a first entry, never an add. Full size once, one stop.
wrong.Raise the stop to breakeven: Breakeven comes at 2R to 5R. Under 1R after 10 trading days, the trade is sold.

questions.simple: Sell it, because a trade still under 1R after 10 trading days has not worked, and the money can go elsewhere.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (C33)

questions.q: Take the break?
questions.story: Lows rise into the falling line for three weeks, and volume fades each day. Today it pokes through.
choices: No; a wedge up, not a tight drift
Yes; it broke the line on the day
Yes; rising lows show demand
No; wait for a close 3% past it
questions.answer: No; a wedge up, not a tight drift
questions.why: No. Our card says rising lows into the line on shrinking volume is not the tight drift down this setup wants. It wants closes tight under the line and a shrinking daily range. A poke through does not change the shape that led into it.
questions.lesson_line: Wedging up into the line is not a tight drift down.

wrong.Yes; it broke the line on the day: Breaking the line is not enough. The shape into it has to be a tight drift down.
wrong.Yes; rising lows show demand: Rising lows into the line on fading volume is wedging up. The card says that is not the drift we want.
wrong.No; wait for a close 3% past it: Our card does not wait for a close 3% past the line. The reason to pass is the wedge up into it.

questions.simple: No, because lows rising into the line on fading volume is a wedge up, not the tight drift down we want.

reasons: rests on a proposed criteria card line awaiting the owner (tl.not_wedging_up)

questions.q: A break gives no price target. What takes its place?
choices: Trims at 3R and 5R, then a trail
The pullback's height, added on top
Sell it all at the old high
Fixed price targets at 2R and 3R
questions.answer: Trims at 3R and 5R, then a trail
questions.why: Trims at 3R and 5R, then a trail. Brandt: the violation of a trendline does not carry with it a price target. So we use our own exits. A third comes off at 3R, a third at 5R, and the last third trails. Our card lists measuring rules and fixed 2R and 3R targets as not ours.
questions.lesson_line: No target from the pattern. The R-based trims do the job.

wrong.The pullback's height, added on top: That is a measuring rule, and the card says measuring rules are not ours. The trims are set in R.
wrong.Sell it all at the old high: The old high is overhead supply, not a target. We trim in thirds and trail the rest.
wrong.Fixed price targets at 2R and 3R: The card lists 2R and 3R targets as not ours. Our trims are a third at 3R and a third at 5R.

questions.simple: We sell a third at 3R and a third at 5R, then trail the rest, because a line break gives no target.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B19, E51, E52)

questions.q: Account 50,000. Risk 0.5%. Buy 109.23, stop 106.79. How many shares?
questions.why: 102. Account times risk percent, divided by the buy minus the stop, then rounded down. That gives 102 shares. Then cap it: the size is the smaller of that and the 40% position cap. Here 102 shares is well under the cap, so 102 stands.
questions.lesson_line: Stop first, distance second, size last.
questions.simple: Buy 102 shares, because the dollars you risk divided by the gap from buy to stop gives that, rounded down.

deeper.example: Raise the risk and the share count rises with it. If the risk-based count ever makes the position bigger than 40% of the account, the 40% cap sets the size instead.

reasons: +2 computed key
+2 rests on the owner's rulebook (A5, A7)
+1 fixed before (risk cut from 1% to 0.5% to stay under the cap)

questions.q: What now?
questions.story: You hold the last third of a fast mover after both trims. Today it closes under its 10-day.
choices: Sell the last third on that close
Hold until the 50-day breaks
Move the stop down for room
Sell if it breaks the 21-day
questions.answer: Sell the last third on that close
questions.why: Sell the last third. Our default trail is the 10-day average for a fast mover and the 21-day for a steadier one. We sell on a close below it. This fast mover closed under its 10-day, so the trail is hit. The stop only moves up, never down.
questions.lesson_line: The trail is a close under the 10-day. Sell it.

wrong.Hold until the 50-day breaks: The trail is the 10-day for a fast mover, not the 50-day.
wrong.Move the stop down for room: The stop only moves up, never down or wider.
wrong.Sell if it breaks the 21-day: The 21-day is the trail for a steadier stock. A fast mover trails the 10-day.

questions.simple: Sell the last third, because a fast mover trails the 10-day and it just closed below that line.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (E52, A4)

questions.q: What now?
questions.story: You bought at 40.00 with the stop at 39.00. It gaps open at 38.20, and the first 30-minute low is 37.80.
choices: Out; the loss is 2.2R, past 2R
New stop at 37.80, the 30-minute low
Hold; a gap like this tends to fill
New stop at 38.20, the opening price
questions.why: Out. On a gap through the stop, the low of the first 30-minute bar is the new stop. The rule has a ceiling: if the first 30 minutes take the loss past 2R, get out. The risk was 40.00 minus 39.00. The low of 37.80 puts the loss at 2.2R, past the ceiling.
questions.lesson_line: A gap through the stop has a ceiling of 2R.

wrong.New stop at 37.80, the 30-minute low: The 30-minute low is the stop only while the loss is inside 2R. At 2.2R this one is past it.
wrong.Hold; a gap like this tends to fill: Hope is not a rule. The gap rule has a ceiling, and this loss is past it.
wrong.New stop at 38.20, the opening price: The rule uses the low of the first 30-minute bar, not the open. And this loss is past 2R.

questions.simple: Get out, because the first 30 minutes took the loss to 2.2R, and past 2R the gap rule says sell.

deeper.example: The risk was 40.00 minus 39.00 a share. The first 30-minute low of 37.80 is 2.2 times that under the buy, so the loss is 2.2R. That is past the 2R ceiling, so you are out. Had the low held inside 2R, it would have become the new stop.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B20 and its ceiling)
computed key (the 2R line)

questions.q: On one stock we allow up to 10 tries a month.
questions.why: False. On one stock we allow at most 3 tries in a week and 6 in a month. After a stop-out, only a new trigger buys it again. Never redraw the same line to get back in.
questions.lesson_line: Cap the tries at 3 a week and 6 a month.
questions.simple: False, we allow at most 3 tries a week and 6 a month on the same stock, not 10.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (E56)
+1 fixed before (replaced a duplicate of q51)

questions.q: Buy it?
questions.story: A clean break sets up for tomorrow. The company reports after the close in 2 days.
choices: No; the report is inside 3 days
Yes; the line is clean
Yes, and sell before it
No; it reports this month
questions.answer: No; the report is inside 3 days
questions.why: No. Our rule: no new buys in the 3 days before an earnings report. A report in 2 days is inside that window, so the break waits. Holding through a report is only for a trade already up 5R. The rule covers those 3 days, not the whole season.
questions.lesson_line: Stay three days clear of the report, or wait.

wrong.Yes; the line is clean: A clean line does not move the earnings window.
wrong.Yes, and sell before it: The rule is no new buy in that window, not a quick trade through it.
wrong.No; it reports this month: The rule is narrower: no new buys in the 3 days before a report. A report this month alone does not block a buy.

questions.simple: No, because we make no new buys in the 3 days before a report, and this one comes in 2 days.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B22)

questions.q: What do you do?
questions.story: You are up 2.5R after three days of a vertical, wide-range climb.
choices: Sell a big part into strength
Add more; it goes parabolic
Hold it all; the trail works
Raise the stop to breakeven
questions.answer: Sell a big part into strength
questions.why: Sell a big part into it. Our rule: a climax run on your own long is for selling a big part into. How much is a judgment call. Adding is never allowed: a break is a first entry, never an add.
questions.lesson_line: A vertical burst is for selling into.

wrong.Add more; it goes parabolic: A break is never an add. A climax run on your own long is for selling into.
wrong.Hold it all; the trail works: Our rule for a climax run is to sell a big part into it, not to leave it all to the trail.
wrong.Raise the stop to breakeven: A breakeven stop protects the cost, not the gain. A climax run is the time to sell a big part.

questions.simple: Sell a big part into strength, because a fast vertical climb on your own stock is for selling into.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (C34, a judgment call)
+1 fixed before

questions.q: What do you do?
questions.story: You bought at 30.00 with the stop at 29.00. It trades to 33.00.
choices: Sell a third; stop to breakeven
Sell half now and trail the rest
Sell a third; widen the stop
Sell it all; 3R is the target
questions.answer: Sell a third; stop to breakeven
questions.why: Sell a third and move the stop to breakeven, 30.00. The risk was 30.00 minus 29.00, so 33.00 is three times that risk above the buy: 3R. Our hard rule takes a third at 3R. The card moves the stop to breakeven at the first trim by default. The next third waits for 5R, and the last third trails.
questions.lesson_line: A third at 3R, then the stop to breakeven.

wrong.Sell half now and trail the rest: The rule is a third at 3R and a third at 5R, not half at once.
wrong.Sell a third; widen the stop: The stop only moves up, never down or wider.
wrong.Sell it all; 3R is the target: 3R is the first trim, not the exit. A third comes off now, a third at 5R, and the rest trails.

questions.simple: Sell a third at 3R and move your stop up to breakeven, because that is our first trim rule.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B19, E51)
computed key (33.00 is 3R)

questions.q: You followed every rule. What was the loss?
questions.story: You bought through an 83-session line at 18.79 with the stop at 18.53. The break closed only 0.39% over the line. Next day the low was 18.39.
choices: A planned loss; the stop did its job
A mistake; the stop was too tight
A reason to redraw the line
questions.answer: A planned loss; the stop did its job
questions.why: A planned loss. The stop is the exit and it did its job. A break that barely clears the line is a weak one.
questions.lesson_line: A stop that trades is the plan working.

wrong.A mistake; the stop was too tight: The stop sits a few cents under the day's low by the rule. Widening it to dodge a loss is the mistake.
wrong.A reason to redraw the line: Redrawing the line to get back in is the named mistake. Only a new trigger buys again.

questions.q: What do you do at the open?
questions.story: You bought at 145.75 with the stop at 144.17, so 3R is 150.49 and 5R is 153.65. The next session opens at 152.00.
choices: Sell a third at the open
Hold; wait for the close
Sell it all at the open
Sell two thirds at the open
questions.answer: Sell a third at the open
questions.why: Sell a third at the open. Our rule: if a stock opens above a trim level, take that trim at the open. The open at 152.00 is past 3R at 150.49, so the first third goes at once. That session then fell to 144.06 and the stop took the rest. The trim had already banked a gain.
questions.lesson_line: Take the trim the open hands you.

wrong.Hold; wait for the close: The level is already passed. Waiting gave the gap time to fill.
wrong.Sell it all at the open: A third at 3R. The rest waits for 5R and the trail.
wrong.Sell two thirds at the open: The open at 152.00 is past 3R at 150.49 but short of 5R at 153.65. Only the first third comes off.

questions.simple: Sell a third right at the open, because the price opened past the 3R trim level, so the trim is already due.

deeper.example: This is EL in December 2018. The buy was 145.75 with the stop at 144.17. The next session opened at 152.00, past 3R, then fell to 144.06, under the stop. Waiting for the close would have handed the whole gap back. The trim at the open banked a third at a profit before the stop took the rest.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (F63)
computed key (3R level in the story)

questions.q: Where is the buy?
questions.story: A stock forms a high tight flag after a sharp run. A falling line crosses the flag's highs.
choices: Over the pattern's highest high
Through the falling line at once
On a dip to the 50-day average
At the flag's low, on weakness
questions.why: Over the pattern's highest high. Our card names this mistake: using the flag's trendline break on a high tight flag. Citing Bulkowski, it says they fail too often that way. A plain flag can use its line as the trigger; a high tight flag buys its highest high.
questions.lesson_line: On a high tight flag, buy the pattern high, not the line.

wrong.Through the falling line at once: On a high tight flag the flag's trendline break fails too often. That is the named mistake.
wrong.At the flag's low, on weakness: Buying the flag's low is buying weakness with no trigger. The buy is on strength, over the pattern's highest high.
wrong.On a dip to the 50-day average: Our buy is on strength over the pattern's highest high, not on a dip to an average.

questions.simple: Buy over the pattern's highest high, because breaks of the flag's line fail too often on a high tight flag.

deeper.trap: A falling line across a flag looks like a trendline break, and the first push through it is tempting. On a high tight flag that early buy fails too often. Wait for price to clear the highest high of the whole pattern.

reasons: +3 one cited fact only (c43; Bulkowski's line is the card's, not quoted from his page)
+2 tied to D-002 (the setup map)

questions.q: You were stopped out. What now?
questions.story: You bought at 200.06 with the stop at 197.41. The next low was 197.22, 19 cents under the stop. It closed at 209.53.
choices: Only a new trigger re-enters
Buy it back at once; it ran 6%
Re-enter now; you get 3 tries
Redraw the line and buy back in
questions.why: Only a new trigger. Our rule: after a stop-out, buy again only if the setup triggers again. It is a new trade with its own stop and every rule. The card adds: do not redraw the same line to get back in. The stock reached 217 within a week. That is the cost of a stop, not a reason to chase.
questions.lesson_line: It ran without you. Only a new trigger buys it back.

wrong.Buy it back at once; it ran 6%: Chasing what ran is the mistake. A re-entry needs a new trigger.
wrong.Re-enter now; you get 3 tries: Three tries a week is a cap, not a license. Each try needs a new trigger.
wrong.Redraw the line and buy back in: The card says do not redraw the same line to get back in. Only a new trigger counts.

questions.simple: Wait for a new trigger, because after a stop-out we only buy again when the setup fires again as a new trade.

deeper.trap: The pain is real: the stop missed by 19 cents and the stock ran to 217 without you. The trap is to fix that feeling by chasing, by redrawing the line, or by treating the 3 tries as free entries. Each one breaks a rule. Only a new trigger brings you back, with its own stop and size.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B21)
the structural stop is held (D-008) and never keyed

questions.q: What does the quiet volume say?
questions.story: A clean line of 3 touches over 85 sessions breaks, but on only 0.86x the 50-day average volume.
choices: Weak; a break with volume matters more
Nothing; volume is noise
Strong; no one is selling
questions.answer: Weak; a break with volume matters more
questions.why: Weak. A trendline break with volume matters more than a break without. This quiet one is a poor sign.
questions.lesson_line: Volume confirms the break. A quiet break is a weak one.

wrong.Nothing; volume is noise: The Insider says a break with volume matters more than one without.
wrong.Strong; no one is selling: Quiet volume on a break is not strength. Buyers did not show up.

questions.q: Take the break?
questions.story: A steep three-week drop leaves two lower highs. A line through them breaks today.
choices: Pass; not the tight drift we want
Take it; the line broke today
Take it, but on half the size
Pass; lower highs, a downtrend
questions.answer: Pass; not the tight drift we want
questions.why: Pass. A steep three-week drop is a drop, not the tight drift down this setup wants. Our card names buying breaks of steep lines as a mistake. ChartSchool says the steeper a trend line, the less valid it is.
questions.lesson_line: A steep plunge draws a steep line. Skip it.

wrong.Take it; the line broke today: The steeper the line, the less valid it is. A break of it is not enough.
wrong.Take it, but on half the size: Size does not repair a steep line drawn off a fast drop.
wrong.Pass; lower highs, a downtrend: Lower highs are what draw a falling line, so they are not the problem. The steep drop is.

questions.simple: Pass, because a fast, steep drop makes a steep line, and that is a drop, not the tight drift we want.

deeper.counter: Compare a real line from our research. MSFT in 2012 drifted tight under a line with 6 touches over 112 sessions, and 3R came the next day. This story is a steep three-week drop with two lower highs. Both are called trendlines, but one is a slow drift and the other is a plunge.

reasons: rests on a proposed criteria card line awaiting the owner (the steep-line mistake)
the slope number is held (D-069) and never keyed

questions.q: The stop traded. Did the rules fail?
questions.story: You buy a clean break at 48.12 with the stop at 47.25. The next session is the first day of a market break, and the stop trades.
choices: No; a planned loss, rules kept
Yes; we should have waited a day
Yes; the stop was too wide
No; rebuy it at the same price
questions.answer: No; a planned loss, rules kept
questions.why: No. The stop is the exit, and it did its job. The next session was the first day of the February 2020 market break. The plan risked 1.80%, and the stop took it out. A valid break can still lose. Another buy needs a new trigger.
questions.lesson_line: A valid break can lose. The stop makes it small.

wrong.Yes; we should have waited a day: Waiting would have been a different trade. This one risked the planned 1.80%, and the stop did its job.
wrong.Yes; the stop was too wide: The stop was 1.80% away, inside the 3% a stop usually sits within.
wrong.No; rebuy it at the same price: The verdict is right, the next step is not. After a stop-out, only a new trigger buys it again.

questions.simple: No, the stop did its job, so the loss was planned and the rules held.

deeper.counter: The stock fell to 34.45 within 10 sessions. Without the stop, the loss would have been far bigger than the 1.80% planned. A rule that loses small on a bad day has done its work.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (A4, B21)
+1 fixed before

questions.q: In our test the stop never moved and no trims were taken. Many reached 3R first, yet 78.8% were stopped. What do we do?
choices: Sell into strength, then trail
Stop trading line breaks
Widen the stop to stay in longer
Drop the stop; let winners run
questions.why: Sell into strength, then trail. In our test the stop never moved and nothing was sold early, and 78.8% were eventually stopped. Many had reached 3R before the stop. That is what a fixed stop without trims does. So we sell a third at 3R, a third at 5R, and trail the rest.
questions.lesson_line: Bank a third at 3R and 5R. Trail the rest.

wrong.Stop trading line breaks: Many reached 3R first, so the entries worked. The exits gave the gains back.
wrong.Widen the stop to stay in longer: The stop never moves down or wider. The test points at the exits, not the stop.
wrong.Drop the stop; let winners run: The stop is the exit and it stays. The fix is to sell into strength at 3R and 5R.

questions.simple: Sell into strength and trail the rest, because a stop that never moves gives back what winners already made.

deeper.trap: Eventually stopped does not mean the idea was wrong. In this test the stop never moved, so a trade could reach 3R and still end at the stop. The exits decide how much of a good entry you keep.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (B19, E51, E52)
+2 a scan statistic from our own data
+1 fixed before (the 54.2% headline removed)

questions.q: Write the plan.
questions.story: A stock trades through its falling line at 30.00 and the prior day's high. You fill at 30.06. The day's low so far is 29.40.
choices: Stop under 29.40; a third at 3R
Stop on the line; third at 3R
Stop under 29.40; all at 3R
Stop on the line; all at 3R
questions.why: Stop a few cents under 29.40, a third off at 3R. The stop goes a few cents under the trigger day's low as it stands at entry, not on the line. A third comes off at 3R, a third at 5R, and the rest trails.
questions.lesson_line: The stop goes under the day's low, not on the line.

wrong.Stop on the line; third at 3R: 30.00 is the line's value, not the stop. The stop goes a few cents under the trigger day's low.
wrong.Stop under 29.40; all at 3R: The stop is right, but only a third comes off at 3R. Another third goes at 5R, and the rest trails.
wrong.Stop on the line; all at 3R: Both parts miss. The stop sits under the day's low, not on the line, and only a third comes off at 3R.

questions.simple: Put the stop a few cents under the day's low of 29.40, not on the line, and sell a third at 3R.

deeper.trap: A stop on the line feels logical, since the line is what broke. But the line is the trigger, not the stop. The stop is a price a few cents under the trigger day's low.

reasons: +2 tied to D-003 (the entry event)
+2 rests on the owner's rulebook (A3, F62, B19)
+1 fixed before

questions.q: Which gets the bigger size?
questions.story: Two valid breaks, months apart. A: a leader tight under the line, room overhead, stop 1.5% away, Green market. B: stop 4% away, a key level just above, Yellow market.
choices: A; all its cues line up
B; it has the wider stop
Equal; the line is the same
Equal; the stop sets size
questions.answer: A; all its cues line up
questions.why: A. A sits tight under the line with room overhead, two A+ cues on our card. It trades in a Green market, where risk is full. B trades in a Yellow market, which means smaller and fewer. Its 4% stop and the key level just above both grade it lower. At the same risk, B's wider stop also means a smaller position.
questions.lesson_line: Same line, different grade. The spot and the market set the size.

wrong.B; it has the wider stop: A wider stop grades it down, and so does the key level just above.
wrong.Equal; the line is the same: The line is the same, but the market, the stop and the room are not.
wrong.Equal; the stop sets size: The stop sets the size, and B's 4% stop gives a smaller position than A's 1.5%. The market and the grade cut B again.

questions.simple: A gets the bigger size. It is tight with room overhead in a Green market, while B has a wider stop in Yellow.

deeper.trap: The trap is thinking a valid break is a valid break. Both lines qualify, so the line does not decide the size. The stock's spot and the market do. At the same risk, B's wider stop alone means a smaller position. The Yellow reading and the key level just above cut it again.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook and the card's grading rows
fixed before (requoted g5)

questions.q: Is this the first break?
questions.story: Last week a stock closed over its falling line, then slid back under. Today it trades through the line again.
choices: No; it already closed through
Yes; a wick is allowed
Yes; each day starts fresh
No; a week is too soon
questions.why: No. A first break has no daily close above the line between the first anchor and the trigger day. A wick through is allowed, a close is not. The close last week spent the first break.
questions.lesson_line: One close over the line spends the first break.

wrong.Yes; a wick is allowed: A wick is allowed, but a close above the line is not. This one closed over it.
wrong.Yes; each day starts fresh: The rule counts closes above the line since the first anchor, not days.
wrong.No; a week is too soon: Our card's rule is about closes, not waiting. One daily close above the line already spent the first break.

questions.simple: No, because the stock already closed above the line last week, and a first break has no earlier close above it.

deeper.trap: A close over the line, a slide back under, then a fresh push can look like a second chance. By the card it is a line already spent. It is not a first break, so it is not this setup's buy.

reasons: +3 one cited fact only (c02)
+2 the card's proposed strict zero; the scanner allows an older close
+1 story reworded in this batch

questions.q: Price reached the start of the line 77% of the time, so we sell all at that old high.
questions.why: False. The old high is overhead supply, context and not a rule. No pattern target replaces the R-based trims.
questions.lesson_line: The old high is supply to respect, not a target.

questions.q: Take the break?
questions.story: A clean break of a long line in a stock with an RS rating of 55, in a lagging group.
choices: No; the stock is not a leader
Yes; the line itself is clean
Yes, with a smaller stop and size
No; a line that long is stale
questions.answer: No; the stock is not a leader
questions.why: No. We buy leaders: an RS rating of 80 or more, in one of the strongest groups. An RS of 55 in a lagging group fails that gate, however clean the line. The exceptions are parabolic and mean-reversion trades, and this is neither.
questions.lesson_line: The stock comes before the line.

wrong.Yes, with a smaller stop and size: A smaller stop does not make a laggard a leader.
wrong.Yes; the line itself is clean: A clean line is only one of the gates. The RS rating is another, and this stock fails it.
wrong.No; a line that long is stale: Line length is not the problem. MSFT drifted tightly under a five-month line. The RS gate is what fails.

questions.simple: No, because we only buy leaders with an RS rating of 80 or more in strong groups, and this one is 55.

deeper.counter: A clean line in a weak stock is the classic trap: the chart looks right, so the stock gets a pass. Run the stock gates first. Price $10 or more and $20 million traded a day. A close above the 200-day. An RS rating of 80 or more in a strong group. Only then look at the line.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (C31)

questions.q: Hidden ticker. A pullback drifts tight under a falling line. Above its 200-day? Take the break or pass.
choices: Take it; it holds above the 200-day
Pass; the stock is under the 200-day
Pass; the share price is too high
Take it, and add more on a dip
questions.answer: Take it; it holds above the 200-day
questions.why: Take it. On the chart the stock closes above its 200-day, which a long needs. The pullback drifts tight under a shallow, slow line. Our research lists this break among its examples, and it ran straight to new highs. It is one buy at full size, never an add.
questions.lesson_line: The 200-day and the tight drift first. Then the line.

wrong.Pass; the stock is under the 200-day: Look again: price sits above the 200-day here.
wrong.Pass; the share price is too high: Our floor is $10 a share and $20 million a day. A high price is no reason to pass.
wrong.Take it, and add more on a dip: A break is a first entry, never an add. Full size once, one stop.

questions.simple: Take it, because the stock is above its 200-day and drifts tight under a slow falling line, which is our setup.

deeper.example: This is MCK in February 2025, a high-priced leader with a shallow, slow line and five touches. The buy filled at 609.84 with the stop at 601.40, 1.4% away. The break ran straight to new highs. A slow line is still a line: it falls a little from lower highs, so it is not a flat top.

reasons: rests on our own research data (one dossier) and the settled 200-day rule

questions.q: Hidden ticker. A good-looking falling line. Is the stock above its 200-day? Take the break or pass.
choices: Pass; it is under the 200-day
Take it; the line is long and clean
Take it; the volume looks fine
Pass; the line is not steep enough
questions.why: Pass. On the trigger day the close was 4.9% under the 200-day, and our rule needs a close above it. A good-looking line under a flat 200-day is not our break. The line's length and the volume do not change that.
questions.lesson_line: A fine line under the 200-day is still a pass.

wrong.Take it; the line is long and clean: A long, clean line is only one gate. The 200-day is another.
wrong.Take it; the volume looks fine: Fine volume does not lift a stock over its 200-day.
wrong.Pass; the line is not steep enough: Steeper is not better. ChartSchool says that as a line gets steeper, its validity decreases. The gate this stock fails is the 200-day.

questions.simple: Pass, because the stock closed under its 200-day on the trigger day, and we buy no longs there.

deeper.trap: A long line with clean touches pulls the eye. Check the 200-day first. If the stock closes under it, the line does not matter for a long.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (B26)
+1 fixed before (the why now names the trigger day)

questions.q: Which one do we take?
questions.story: Four breaks today. A: under its 200-day. B: reports in 2 days. C: a leader, tight under the line. D: gaps 5% over the line.
choices: A; the 200-day is a soft rule
B; sell it before the report
C; no gate here rules it out
D; the gap shows strength
questions.answer: C; no gate here rules it out
questions.why: C. Each of the others fails a gate. A sits under its 200-day, and we take no longs below it unless parabolic. B reports in 2 days, inside the 3 days before a report when we make no new buys. D gaps 5% over the line, and a gap open more than 4% above the line is no trade. C is the leader tight under the line, and nothing here rules it out.
questions.lesson_line: Run every gate. One failure ends it.

questions.q: If you wait and buy that close, what changes?
choices: Fewer shares for the same risk
More risk on the trade, same shares
A tighter stop and more shares

questions.answer: Fewer shares for the same risk
questions.why: Fewer shares. Our card does not wait for a close 3% past the line. It would use up most of the 4% chase limit and widen the stop. Chasing costs size, not risk. The stop stays under the buy point, so the distance grows and the shares shrink.
questions.lesson_line: Waiting for a 3% close widens the stop and shrinks the shares.

wrong.More risk on the trade, same shares: Chasing costs size, not risk. The risk stays the same, so the shares shrink.
wrong.A tighter stop and more shares: It is the reverse. A higher buy widens the stop, so the same risk buys fewer shares.
wrong.Nothing; only the price is higher: A higher buy with the stop still under the buy point widens the distance. The shares shrink.

questions.simple: You get fewer shares, because a higher buy puts the stop farther away, and the risk stays the same.

deeper.counter: The classic 3% close was built for long-term lines, where a small poke through can mean little. Our lines are short-term, and we never buy more than 4% above the buy point. A 3% wait uses up most of that room before you even buy.
